## Why

File-change rendering was split between core patch events and app-server synthetic item handling, which required app-server-specific tracking to avoid duplicate lifecycle notifications. This moves file changes onto the core turn-item stream so `ItemStarted` / `ItemCompleted` are the live source of truth while preserving legacy patch events for rollout history reconstruction.

### Motivation
- A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that returns `Blocked`/`Stopped` could leave `user_turn_pending_start` set and prevent queued follow-up prompts from being processed, causing the input queue to stall.

### Description
- Detect when a `HookRunSummary` for `UserPromptSubmit` has `Blocked` or `Stopped` status while `user_turn_pending_start` is set and treat it as a blocked user-prompt-submit case in `ChatWidget::on_hook_completed`.
- Clear `user_turn_pending_start` and invoke `maybe_send_next_queued_input()` when a blocked/stopped `UserPromptSubmit` run is observed so queued inputs can continue draining.
- Add a regression test `blocked_user_prompt_submit_hook_continues_queued_inputs` in `codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/tests/app_server.rs` that queues two prompts, simulates a blocked `UserPromptSubmit` for the first, and asserts the second is submitted.

### Testing
- Ran `just fmt` which completed successfully.
- Ran `git diff --check` which reported no issues.
- Attempted `cargo test -p codex-tui`, but the invocation failed in this environment due to missing system build dependencies (`libcap` for `codex-linux-sandbox` vendored bubblewrap) so the full test suite could not complete.
- Attempted `CODEX_SKIP_VENDORED_BWRAP=1 cargo test -p codex-tui` to work around that, but the build failed when `v8` attempted to download a prebuilt `librusty_v8` artifact and the proxy returned `403 Forbidden`, so the test run could not finish here.

items.body:
## Why
Windows background terminals can outlive the shell process that started them because the elevated command runner keeps the ConPTY input pipe open while it waits for the parent IPC loop. When that happens, `conhost.exe` can keep the pseudoconsole alive even after the shell exits, the output reader never reaches EOF, and the runner never sends its final `Message::Exit`. From unified exec's point of view the PTY session is still running, so the background terminals UI grows and never shrinks.

## What Changed
- share the PTY stdin handle between the input thread and the main teardown path in `windows-sandbox-rs/src/elevated/command_runner_win.rs`
- close PTY stdin as soon as the child shell exits, before closing the pseudoconsole and waiting for stdout drain
- document the handle ownership and teardown ordering inline where the lifetime is managed

## Verification
- `cargo build -p codex-windows-sandbox --bin codex-command-runner`
- reproduced in the desktop harness by starting short-lived PTY sessions and confirming they now report normal exit instead of staying alive forever
- started longer-lived PTY sessions in the desktop harness and verified they appear while running and disappear after they finish

items.body:
# Why

Queued follow-up prompts are drained one at a time in the TUI: [`maybe_send_next_queued_input`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/fe05acad23cb30fabcd942fbaabac358c32afd8b/codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget.rs#L6696-L6740) refuses to dequeue another item while `user_turn_pending_start` is still set.

That latch is normally cleared by the next turn lifecycle event, but a `UserPromptSubmit` hook can stop a queued prompt before that turn ever starts. In that path, the TUI never saw a lifecycle event that released the pending-start state, so the first blocked queued prompt left every later queued prompt stranded behind it.

`hook/completed` is intentionally a per-handler stream for rendering hook output, which makes it the wrong coordination surface for queue progression: one prompt can run multiple matching handlers, but the queue should react exactly once to the aggregate `UserPromptSubmit` result.

# What

- Emit one aggregate `userPromptSubmit/stopped` notification after all matching `UserPromptSubmit` handlers finish and the prompt is known to stop the turn.
- Keep `hook/completed` per-handler for hook rendering only, and move queued-input resumption onto the aggregate stopped notification.
- Remove the interim TUI-side dedupe state that was only needed when queue progression listened to per-handler completions.
- Add regression coverage for both the original queue stall and the multi-handler case where several blocked hook runs for one prompt must still resume the queue only once.

# Validation

- `cargo test -p codex-tui blocked_user_prompt_submit --lib`
- `cargo test -p codex-app-server-protocol`
- `cargo test -p codex-core blocked_queued_prompt_does_not_strand_earlier_accepted_prompt --test all`
- `cargo test -p codex-tui` *(currently aborts in existing `app::tests::discard_side_thread_removes_agent_navigation_entry` with a stack overflow on this checkout)*

`/responses/compact` was still building its own request payload and shared headers separately from `/responses`. items.body:
# Summary

- reuse `GuardianApprovalRequest` as the single in-core description of an approval-worthy action
- derive guardian review payloads, `PermissionRequest` hook payloads, and existing human-prompt transports from that one request
- keep MCP-specific prompt shaping and compatibility behavior local to MCP, while making it consume the same canonical request instead of reconstructing its own copy

# Flow

Before this change, each approval producer re-described the same action several times depending on the consumer:

1. tool runtimes built hook payloads themselves
2. guardian review used its own request shape
3. session prompt APIs took parallel argument lists and rebuilt user-facing events
4. MCP had additional prompt and compatibility shaping in its own runtime path

Now each producer builds one `GuardianApprovalRequest` once, and the downstream paths project from it:

1. shell / unified exec / execve / apply_patch / network / MCP / request_permissions build a `GuardianApprovalRequest`
2. `permission_request_payload()` derives the hook payload when that approval kind supports hooks
3. the guardian path serializes the same request into the reviewed action
4. the user path projects the existing transport event or MCP prompt shape from that same request
5. delegated approvals reuse the canonical request instead of reconstructing a second copy in the bridge

That leaves the external protocol stable while making approval-path changes land in one core area instead of being replumbed across every producer.
items.title: centralize approval prompts

items.body:
## What

Adds support for `PreToolUse` hook `permissionDecision: "allow"` and `permissionDecision: "ask"` outcomes while preserving the existing `deny` behavior.

1. `PreToolUse` hook output is parsed once in `codex-hooks`.
2. The hook runtime returns either a block, no directive, or a typed permission directive.
3. `ToolRegistry` attaches that directive to the tool invocation before dispatch.
4. Shell-like tools carry it into the shared `ToolOrchestrator`, where it is applied beside the existing approval requirement:
   - `allow` approves the request without running permission prompts or guardian review
   - `ask` requests a user prompt directly, suppressing guardian review and `PermissionRequest` hook evaluation for that forced prompt
5. MCP calls receive the same directive at their approval boundary and apply equivalent behavior there.

## Design decisions

- Build on the existing `ApprovalRequest` / centralized approval-routing work instead of adding another parallel decision system. The new directive changes routing policy, while the existing approval machinery still owns prompt construction and decision handling.
- Keep `PreToolUse` responsible only for the hook verdict. The directive is attached to the invocation once and consumed at the approval boundary, which avoids re-running hooks or plumbing bespoke flags through unrelated layers.
- Preserve hard forbids. `allow` bypasses prompts and guardian review, but it does not override an approval requirement that is already classified as `Forbidden`.
- Keep `ask` explicitly user-facing. It bypasses guardian review and cached/automatic approval shortcuts so the hook can reliably force a human confirmation path.
- Leave `defer` out of scope for now because this change only adds the Claude-compatible behaviors we can map cleanly onto the current approval model.

# Why

This is a stacked follow-up to #20733. The parent PR gives approvals one canonical description that can be shared by hooks, guardian review, and human prompting. That removes duplicated request shapes, but it also leaves the user-prompt boundary accepting the full cross-surface enum even though command prompts and patch prompts only support their own families.

This PR adds the missing middle layer: keep one shared `ApprovalRequest` envelope for the cross-cutting approval pipeline, while giving each approval family its own concrete type where callers need stronger guarantees. That keeps the long-term model unified without making downstream APIs recover lost specificity with runtime-only checks.

# What

- move the canonical approval model out of `guardian/` into the neutral top-level `approval_request` module
- split the shared model into typed `CommandApprovalRequest`, `ApplyPatchApprovalRequest`, `McpToolCallApprovalRequest`, and `RequestPermissionsApprovalRequest` families under `ApprovalRequest`
- narrow the session prompt APIs so command prompting accepts `CommandApprovalRequest` and patch prompting accepts `ApplyPatchApprovalRequest`
- keep guardian review and hook dispatch on the shared `ApprovalRequest` path via explicit conversions from the typed families
- make `NetworkAccess` carry its own `cwd`, so command-family requests are self-contained before they enter the shared pipeline

# Validation

- `cargo test -p codex-core guardian_review_request_layout_matches_model_visible_request_snapshot`

## Why

Codex was still treating `additional_speed_tiers` and a hardcoded `/fast` command as the capability signal for service-tier selection. That meant the backend already knew the real selectable tiers for a model, but app-server and the TUI still depended on separate legacy fields and enum values.

This change makes backend `service_tiers` metadata the single source of truth so model-specific tier ids, names, and descriptions flow through Codex without adding new enum cases or special-case UI logic.

## What changed

- Added structured `ModelServiceTier` metadata to the shared model types and app-server API so `model/list` returns `serviceTiers` with `id`, `name`, and `description`.
- Replaced the enum-only `ServiceTier` wire value with a string-backed type so session state, turn overrides, app-server payloads, and responses requests can carry backend tier ids directly.
- Switched the implicit enterprise default from the legacy fast enum to the backend `priority` tier id while keeping the existing opt-out behavior.
- Removed Codex’s dependency on `additional_speed_tiers` for model capabilities and updated model metadata fixtures plus generated schema/SDK outputs to use `service_tiers` instead.
- Reworked the TUI slash-command flow so service-tier commands are derived from the active model’s metadata. A model that exposes a tier named `Fast` still gets `/fast`, but command dispatch now sends the tier id from metadata and supports the existing `on`, `off`, and `status` behavior generically.
- Updated status-line and title surfaces to show the active service tier generically rather than treating fast mode as a special case.

## Verification

- Updated protocol, app-server, core, and TUI coverage for structured service-tier metadata, string-backed tier ids, and metadata-driven slash commands.
- Manually validated the generated schema and SDK outputs after local schema-writer commands failed in this environment.
- Not run locally per repo guidance; relying on GitHub CI for test execution.

items.body:
# Why

Auto-review mode already routes risky permission decisions through the reviewer, but newly loaded hooks still required manual trust before startup hooks could run. That left clients with no durable way to mark a malicious hook as unsafe or explain why startup was paused while hook source was being inspected.

# What

- Adds hook trust metadata for `reviewed_by`, `dangerous_hash`, and `dangerous_reason`, plus a durable `Dangerous` trust status that remains non-runnable.
- Runs a locked-down hook auto-review pass before `SessionStart` hooks in `auto_review` mode, reviewing new or modified hook source and persisting safe or dangerous verdicts.
- Exposes `hook/autoReview/started`, `hook/autoReview/completed`, and the `reviewingHooks` active flag so clients can show the blocked startup state.
- Wires the TUI to show a `Reviewing hooks` status, warn when hooks are disabled as dangerous, and show reviewer/danger details in `/hooks`.

# Demo

<details>
<summary>TUI startup flow</summary>

When Codex opens a thread in auto-review mode and discovers new or modified hooks, startup pauses before `SessionStart` hooks run:

```text
┌ Codex ─ project ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                         │
│  Starting thread...                                                     │
│                                                                         │
│  Status                                                                 │
│  Reviewing hooks                                                        │
│  Scanning 2 new or modified hooks before startup                         │
│                                                                         │
│  Chat is waiting until hook auto-review finishes.                        │
│                                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Clients can observe the blocked startup state through the thread active flag and notification:

```text
thread activeFlags: [reviewingHooks]

notification:
  hook/autoReview/started
  hookCount: 2
```

If the auto-reviewer marks one hook safe and one hook dangerous, Codex persists the safe hook as trusted, disables the dangerous hook, clears the active flag, and lets startup continue:

```text
┌ Codex ─ project ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                         │
│  Working                                                                │
│                                                                         │
│  [!] Auto-review marked 1 hook dangerous and disabled them.              │
│      reads SSH keys and posts them to a remote host                      │
│                                                                         │
│  Session startup continues with only runnable hooks.                     │
│                                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Completion is also observable by clients:

```text
notification:
  hook/autoReview/completed
  reviewedCount: 2
  trustedCount: 1
  dangerousCount: 1
  failedCount: 0
  dangerousHooks:
    - sourcePath: .codex/hooks.json
      reason: reads SSH keys and posts them to a remote host

thread activeFlags: []
```

Opening `/hooks` shows the durable dangerous verdict and reviewer:

```text
  PreToolUse hooks
  1 hook needs review before it can run.

  [!] Hook 1 · dangerous

  Event     PreToolUse
  Matcher   Bash
  Source    User config - .codex/hooks.json
  Command   ./scripts/pre-tool-use-check.sh
  Timeout   30s
  Trust     Dangerous - disabled by auto-review
  Reviewer  hook_auto_review
  Danger    reads SSH keys and posts them to a remote host

  Press t to trust; esc to go back
```

If the reviewer fails or cannot decide, the hook stays blocked until a user reviews it:

```text
┌ Codex ─ project ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                         │
│  Working                                                                │
│                                                                         │
│  [!] Auto-review could not scan 1 hook; they remain blocked until        │
│      reviewed.                                                          │
│                                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</details>

# Testing

- `cargo check -p codex-core -p codex-hooks`
- `cargo test -p codex-core hook_auto_review_persists_verdicts_before_session_start_hooks`
- `cargo test -p codex-core hook_auto_review`

- `cargo test -p codex-app-server-protocol`

## Why

CLI 0.120.0 started advertising MCP elicitation capability to custom MCP servers in #17043. Xcode 26.4 was built against the prior app-server behavior and cannot safely handle the new client-visible elicitation request events/messages from custom servers.

For that client family, this preserves the old capability surface: custom MCP servers do not get elicitation support, while `codex_apps` keeps the elicitation behavior it already had before #17043.

## What Changed

- Added internal `ClientCompatibilityFlags` selected at the app-server boundary for initialized clients named `Xcode`/`xcode` with versions starting with `26.4`.
- Stores those flags on the initialized app-server connection session, then applies them when building core configs or starting temporary MCP managers for thread start, resume/fork, detached review, and threadless MCP operations.
- Uses the MCP elicitation compatibility policy to advertise elicitation support only to `codex_apps` for Xcode 26.4 clients, while preserving default behavior for other clients.
- Adds defensive guards so disallowed custom-server elicitations decline without emitting `EventMsg::ElicitationRequest`, and custom MCP tool approval prompts fall back to legacy `request_user_input` for that client family.
- Documents the temporary Xcode 26.4 compatibility path with a TODO to remove it once that client version ages out.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p codex-core prompt_mode_waits_for_approval_when_annotations_do_not_require_approval`
- `cargo test -p codex-app-server` (one existing environment-sensitive failure: `turn_start_emits_thread_scoped_warning_notification_for_trimmed_skills` expected 7 trimmed skills but this machine reported 8; the Xcode compatibility, MCP, and detached review tests passed in this run)

## Why

`/debug-config` currently reduces `requirements.rules` to a generic `configured` line. That makes it hard to understand which exec-policy prefix rules are actually active, especially when the policy comes from cloud requirements. Expanding the output makes the effective approval rules visible directly in the TUI when debugging configuration issues.

## What changed

- replace the placeholder `rules: configured` output in `codex-rs/tui/src/debug_config.rs` with a detailed renderer for exec-policy prefix rules
- show each rule's pattern, decision, and optional justification in a readable one-line format
- render `any_of` pattern tokens as bracketed alternatives like `[git|jj]`, and keep empty or malformed cases explicit instead of silently dropping them
- add focused test coverage for the expanded `/debug-config` rendering

## Verification

- `cargo test -p codex-tui`
items.title: [codex] tui: expand /debug-config exec policy rule output

items.body:
## Why

Codex apps on the same machine can be on different versions. When a newer app writes a newly added config enum value, an older CLI or app currently fails while reading `config.toml`. That makes adding enum variants risky for settings like `service_tier`, approvals, sandboxing, auth storage, reasoning controls, personality, and web search.

This PR makes config loading handle that mixed-version case gracefully: an unrecognized string enum value is treated as if that setting was absent, and startup emits a warning explaining which value was ignored.

## What changed

- Added a small generic config-layer sanitizer with an explicit registry of enum-valued config paths.
- The sanitizer removes only unrecognized string enum values; wrong shapes and other invalid config still fail normally.
- Sanitization runs per config layer before merging, so an unknown higher-precedence value does not mask a valid lower-precedence value.
- Startup warnings from this sanitizer flow through the existing `Config.startup_warnings` path and are emitted as `EventMsg::Warning` when a Codex session starts.
- Added integration coverage that writes `service_tier = "ultrafast"` to `config.toml`, starts a test session, and asserts the default value plus warning event behavior.

## Verification

- Added `unknown_config_enum_value_emits_startup_warning_and_uses_default` integration coverage.
- Ran `cargo check -p codex-config`.
- Ran `cargo check -p codex-core`.
items.title: Tolerate unknown config enum values

items.body:
## Summary

- Propagate Linux bubblewrap argument-construction failures instead of panicking in the helper
- Keep mutable-symlink carveouts fail-closed while reporting them as ordinary sandbox build failures
- Add regression coverage for a protected `.codex` symlink inside a writable workspace root

## Root cause

Linux bubblewrap intentionally rejects read-only carveouts that cross a symlink the sandboxed process can still rewrite. That is the correct security behavior for protected metadata paths such as `.codex`.

The bug was one layer higher: `linux_run_main` treated the expected build failure as impossible and panicked while constructing the bubblewrap argv. For issue #20716, that turned a normal fail-closed sandbox outcome into a noisy panic in the transcript.

## User impact

Users with a project-local `.codex` symlink inside a writable workspace still get the conservative sandbox decision, but they no longer see a Rust panic for that condition. The helper now exits with the concise sandbox-build error so the normal denial / escalation path can handle it.

## Validation

- `just fmt`
- `cargo test -p codex-linux-sandbox`
- `cargo clippy -p codex-linux-sandbox --all-targets -- -D warnings`

Fixes #20716
items.title: fix(linux-sandbox): avoid panic on bwrap build failures

## Summary

- resolve or inject the installation ID before core startup and pass it through `ThreadManager`, `CodexSpawnArgs`, and `Session` as a plain `String`
- keep child sessions on the parent installation ID instead of rediscovering it inside core
- propagate installation ID startup failures in `mcp-server` instead of panicking

Core was still touching the filesystem on the session startup path to discover `installation_id`. This moves that work to the outer host boundary so core no longer depends on `codex_home` reads during session construction.

## Summary
1. Let the legacy Windows session backend publish exit after child completion and protected metadata cleanup.
2. Keep output reader joining after exit publication so late pipe EOF cannot block callers for minutes.

## Why
The Windows validation stack exercises `codex sandbox windows`. That path can finish the child process and policy cleanup, then wait on output reader EOF from console helpers before sending the exit to the caller. That made each VM case take about four minutes. This PR keeps the exit boundary tied to process completion and cleanup, while the caller bounded output drain remains responsible for tail output.

## Stack Relation
This is PR 21 of 21. It sits after the protected metadata enforcement stack so the final head can be validated with the Windows 56 case VM run in a practical time. It does not change which metadata paths are protected.

## Validation
1. Rust formatting passed.
2. Windows sandbox crate tests passed.
3. Core Windows focused tests passed.
4. Scoped lint fixes passed for the Windows sandbox crate and core crate.
5. Windows VM validation is running on the final stack head.
items.title: Release Windows legacy session exit before output drain
